title: The Stranger Rock: Read a Glacial Erratic Without Guessing Its Origin
subtitle: A boulder can record movement through a landscape. Learn to separate what you can see from what geology can actually show.
imageAlt: Two friends pause beside a large boulder on a public trail, comparing a field notebook with a regional geologic map.
imageConcept: Two friends at a public trail overlook examine a solitary boulder from a respectful distance, one holding an open notebook and the other studying a folded geologic map; the surrounding landscape gives the rock context without implying a definite route.
body: A boulder is a clue, not a caption

A large rock sitting among unfamiliar surroundings can seem to tell a tidy story: it came from somewhere else, traveled on ice, and stopped here. Sometimes that is broadly right. But appearance alone cannot establish where a boulder began, which force moved it, or the exact route it followed. The useful skill is not making the most confident guess. It is learning to keep observation, interpretation and uncertainty distinct.

Geologists call rocks transported by glaciers and deposited far from their source bedrock glacial erratics. Comparing an erratic with bedrock elsewhere can help researchers investigate past ice movement. The National Park Service describes how such rocks can reveal routes that are not obvious from the present-day landscape. That makes a solitary boulder a compelling piece of evidence—but not a complete journey in stone [1].

Treat this as a field exercise for two friends at a public site: look carefully, make separate notes, and then compare the observations with a local geologic map. The goal is not to identify a rock on sight. It is to ask better questions, and to notice what would take more evidence to answer.
Begin with what the eye can record

Choose a boulder that can be viewed safely from a trail or other public area. Do not climb on it, chip it, dig around it or leave the marked route to reach it. Before consulting a map, take two or three minutes to describe the scene independently. Separate what you can directly observe from what you think it means.

Record the boulder’s approximate size in ordinary terms—waist-high, car-sized, or larger than a person—rather than pretending to make a precise measurement. Note its visible colors, grain, layers, crystal shapes, cracks and weathered surfaces. Describe its position: exposed at the surface, partly buried, near a slope, or among rocks of similar size. Include the setting and date, and take a photograph from a permitted viewpoint if photography is allowed.

Then compare notes. One person may notice a banded pattern the other missed; one may call the surface smooth where the other sees angular edges. That disagreement is useful. It shows how quickly a description can turn into an interpretation. “Light-colored rock with dark bands” is an observation. “A piece of distant mountain carried here by a glacier” is a hypothesis that needs supporting evidence.
Ask whether the rock is truly out of place

A boulder can look unusual because the surrounding material is different, but that impression is not a geological diagnosis. The rock may be part of local bedrock, or it may have arrived through a process other than the one a visitor first imagines. Even if transport by ice is plausible in the region, the visible rock does not identify its source or tell you when and how it moved.

This is why the field note should have separate headings: “What we saw,” “What the map suggests,” and “What remains uncertain.” Under the first, keep to visible details. Under the second, record the map’s evidence and what it makes plausible. In the last, write down the unanswered questions: Is the rock type distinctive? Is there a known source area? Could later geological processes have affected where it is exposed?

Keeping those categories apart does not make the outing less adventurous. It protects the adventure from turning into a story that the evidence cannot carry.
Let the map narrow the possibilities

Find a geologic map for the specific area, ideally from a state or provincial geological survey or another established geological agency. Check its legend before interpreting its colors: map units represent particular materials or geological features, and the labels matter more than the palette. A general road map or terrain map may help with location, but it cannot substitute for a map of geology.

Locate the boulder and note what the map says about nearby surface deposits and exposed bedrock. Then look for mapped units that might offer a comparison. Ask what the map actually supports: Does it show a likely local source? Does it indicate material deposited by glaciers? Is the map broad-scale enough that a single boulder would not be represented? Keep the map’s scale and purpose in view. A regional map can orient an investigation without identifying one individual rock.

If you cannot find a useful map, write that down instead of filling the gap with a guess. You can still make a strong field record: describe the setting, save the map name and date if you consulted one, and list the information you would need next. A careful “not enough information yet” is a result, not a failure.

Once a possible source is identified, it is tempting to draw a direct line from that place to the boulder. Research shows why that can oversimplify the story. A 2025 study of erratic dispersal associated with the British–Irish Ice Sheet models possible pathways while accounting for changing ice-flow directions. The researchers caution against assuming that a boulder traveled directly from its source to its resting place [2].

For a visitor, the practical lesson is simple: a map may suggest a broad relationship, but it does not reveal the whole journey. Ice-flow patterns can shift over time, and a route reconstructed from geological evidence is more complex than a single arrow. Keep your own map marks modest. A question mark or shaded area is more honest than a confident line when the evidence does not resolve the route.

You do not need to reproduce a scientific model to benefit from this idea. Just notice the difference between “this source area is a possibility” and “this rock traveled from here along this exact path.” The first may be a useful inference; the second requires evidence your brief visit is unlikely to provide.
A visual match is only the start

Even matching a boulder to a possible source can involve more than appearance. In a 2025 study, researchers measured cosmogenic beryllium-10 in five quartzite boulders near Wamego, Kansas. Their interpretation considered the results alongside the boulders’ exhumation histories. The work illustrates how reconstructing a boulder’s history can require evidence and context beyond a visual comparison [3].

That does not mean every outing needs laboratory analysis. It means you should know what kind of claim your evidence can support. A field description can establish visible features. A geological map can identify nearby units and suggest regional context. More specific conclusions about origin, timing or route may require specialist identification, additional field evidence or scientific methods that are not available to a casual observer.

If the rock is part of a documented local site, read the official interpretation and note its source. Treat it as context rather than a prompt to retrofit your observations. If the site has no posted information, resist filling the silence with certainty. A photograph and a careful question can be more valuable than a label you made up.
Leave with a better field note

Before you go, write a short summary together: “We saw…” followed by concrete features; “The map suggests…” followed by the mapped context; and “We cannot tell…” followed by the open questions. Add the map title or agency, the location, the date and any site interpretation you consulted. If your descriptions differed, keep both versions rather than forcing agreement.

Later, you can check whether a local geological survey, museum or park authority publishes information about the site. Look for explanations tied to the specific boulder or region, and distinguish them from broad descriptions of glacial erratics. If you share a photograph, avoid presenting a suspected origin as fact. A caption such as “Could this be an erratic? Here is what we observed and what the local map shows” invites discussion without overstating the evidence.

The point is not to leave the trail with a complete route map. It is to come away with a more precise sense of what the landscape reveals—and what it keeps to itself. A stranger rock can open a history of movement, but the best fieldwork begins by letting the evidence set the limits of the story.
